documentation.range: The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is considered the most widespread Neotropical freshwater stingray, present in almost the entire distribution range of the subfamily. This species is found in the Amazon, Orinoco, Essequibo, Tocantins, Xingu, Tapajós, Madeira and La Plata basins or part of these basins, including their major tributaries (Lasso et al. 2013, Loboda and Carvalho 2013, Loboda et al. 2016, Fontenelle et al. 2021). The lectotype locality for this species is the Guaporé River, in the Madeira basin (Loboda and Carvalho 2013). This species was taken by the ornamental trade and has been reported as becoming an invasive species in Indonesia (Java Island, Brantas River) (Jerikho et al. 2023) and Singapore (Upper Seletar Reservoir) (Ng et al. 2010). It has also been reported as a potential invasive species for China (Xiong et al. 2015), but has not yet been recorded in the wild in China.
documentation.population: There is no information about population fragmentation, but fishing pressure has been increasingly affecting population sizes in part of its range area. In the La Plata River basin, despite the recent increase in fishing efforts, the population of Ocellate Freshwater Stingray presented a stable trend (Lucifora et al. 2017). In parts of the Amazon Basin (lower Purus River, mid-low Solimões-Amazonas River, mainly along most tributary mouth areas in the Amazon River, such as Tapajós, Xingu, Tocantins-Araguaia), fisheries for food targeting subadults and adults are certainly affecting part of this species population (Araújo 2004, Charvet-Almeida and Almeida 2008) and a suspected decline could reach at least 30%. Overall, considering that in most of its range the population is stable or not severely affected by fishing pressure while reductions may have occurred in parts of its range, the population is suspected of having undergone a population reduction of ~10–19% over the past three generation lengths (29 years).
documentation.habitats: The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is only known to date from freshwater habitat. It was one of the first and most studied species regarding its biology (Thorson et al. 1983) and genetics (Torres et al. 2022). Populations of Ocellate Freshwater Stingray are found in many different kinds of habitats across its entire distribution range, with no apparent habitat preference. It is found mostly in the mid and lower parts of tributaries, and has not often been observed in headwaters. Maximum size varies regionally and is ~50–60 cm disc width (DW) (Lasso et al. 2013, Loboda et al. 2016). Sexual maturation, fecundity and size-at-birth varies across its range. In the Amazon River Basin, males mature at ~39 cm DW and females at ~44 cm DW (Charvet-Almeida et al. 2005). Reproduction is viviparous with an annual reproductive cycle, and average fecundity of 7 pups per litter which can vary between 4–11 pups per litter and size-at-birth is 10–14 cm DW (Charvet-Almeida et al. 2005, Lasso et al. 2013). In the Parana-Paraguay Basin, maturity is reached at ~30–35 cm DW and at ~3 years of age. Fecundity varies between 3–21 pups per litter, and size at birth varies between 9.5–13.5 cm DW (Drioli and Chiaramonte 2009). The age of maturity was estimated as 3–4 years for males and 4–5 years for females (Araujo and Lessa 2015). Generation length was estimated as 9.7 years (Lucifora et al. 2022).
documentation.threats:
The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is subject to a range of habitat degradation impacts across its range, predominantly driven by mining, deforestation, damming, urbanization, and agricultural expansion. The presence of elemental mercury contamination resulting from legal and illegal mining activities has been documented in the Tapajós River (RAISG 2020) and Xingu River (Ribeiro et al. 2017). The deforestation that has occurred throughout the Amazon River Main Channel is known to have impacted the diversity of fish species (Arantes et al. 2018), which is likely to also have a negative effect on the Ocellate Freshwater Stingray population. Moreover, the increase in oil transportation via the Amazon River has given rise to concerns regarding the contamination potential by oil leaks in great part of its distribution area (Esterhuyse et al. 2022, Araujo et al. 2023).

The expansion of agricultural activities in multiple regions of the Amazon Basin represents another significant threat, as it has been linked to increased siltation and contamination from agricultural runoff (Torres 2023). In the Orinoco River Basin, oil extraction (Torremorell et al. 2021) and mining (Ebus and Martinelli 2022) represent significant sources of pollutants. The Paraná-Prata region exhibits a heterogeneous distribution of habitat degradation pressures. The upper areas of the Paraná-Prata River exhibit less impacted habitats, characterized by reduced fishing pressure and minimal habitat degradation. Meanwhile, the lower region is subjected to the combined impacts of fishing and habitat degradation (Lucifora et al. 2017). Moreover, this species is threatened by commercial fishing in the Amazon River Main Channel (Santos 2022). The Ocellate Freshwater stingray is exposed to ornamental fishing (Prang 2020a), being one of the most exported freshwater stingrays from Colombia with 81,109 individuals reported exported in the period between 1999–2011 (Lasso et al. 2013). Therefore, the extraction of juveniles and adults for the international ornamental aquarium trade was considered the main threat for the species in Colombia (Lasso et al. 2013). Negative fishing (sensu Compagno and Cook 1995) is another threat that has also been recorded to occur unevenly throughout the species distribution range (Araújo et al. 2005, Lucifora et al. 2017).
documentation.measures: The Potamotrygoninae subfamily (referred as Potamotrygonidae) was listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) Appendix III in 2017 mainly to improve trade data (CITES 2017). The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray was included in this listing as one of the priority species to be monitored (CITES 2017). The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray was not listed in the recent addition of Potamotrygon species under CITES Appendix II (CITES 2022). The ornamental trade of the Ocellate Freshwater Stingray in Brazil is subject to certain regulatory measures. Export quotas were established limiting international trade to 4,000 specimens per year from the Amazonas State and 1,200 from Pará State. The same regulatory measures established a maximum export size of 30 cm disc width (Ramos 2017). It has been reported that individuals of other potamotrygonins species (such as Reticulated Freshwater Stingray, P. falkneri; Pearl Freshwater Stingray, P. jabuti; Henle's Freshwater Stingray, P. henlei; and Xingu Freshwater Stingray P. leopoldi) have been exported under the label of Ocellate Freshwater Stingray as a means of circumventing the established exportation limits and prohibitions (Araújo et al. 2004; Ramos 2017; Prang 2020a,b).
documentation.use_trade: The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is targeted for consumption, being one of the most captured species in commercial fishing throughout the Amazon River and most major tributaries across the Amazon Basin. It is captured by different gears, mostly longline and seine nets, but also by trawling and spearing. Adult and subadult individuals predominate in catch composition. Captured fish are usually traded in Brazilian fish markets within the Amazon Region but are also taken to be traded as far as the southeast portions of Brazil, sometimes as marine skates and other Rajiformes (Camacho-Oliveira et al. 2020). This species has been exported to Asia (mainly Japan and South Korea) as Rajiformes, both as dried and frozen fillets (Araujo 2004, Charvet et al. 2022, Oliveira et al. 2023). Furthermore, the species is a target for the international ornamental aquarium trade, representing the most exported potamotrygonin species for ornamental purposes from Brazil (Duncan et al. 2010) and Colombia (Lasso et al. 2013). The species is identified in the ornamental market by the following codes: P1, P2, P3, P5, P32, P33, P34, P35, P36, P37, P38, P39, P40, P41, P44, P45, P46, P47, P48, P49 (Ross and Schaffer 2000). Furthermore, the Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is a target species for the production of hybrids with other potamotrygonin species, including Xingu Freshwater Stingray (Potamotrygon leopoldi), Pearl Freshwater Stingray (Potamotrygon jabuti), and Wallace's Freshwater Stingray (Potamotrygon wallacei) (Prang 2020a).
documentation.rationale: The Ocellate Freshwater Stingray (Potamotrygon motoro) is a small to medium sized (to 60 cm disc width) Neotropical freshwater stingray. It is the most widespread Neotropical freshwater stingray and occurs in several of the main South American river basins, including the Amazon, Orinoco, Essequibo, Tocantins-Araguaia, Xingú, Tapajós, Madeira basins and Paraná-La Plata regions. Moreover, this species was taken to Southeast Asia by the international ornamental aquarium trade, was released or escaped to wild habitats and became an invasive species in Indonesia and Singapore. In its natural habitat this species has an annual reproductive cycle and an average of 7 pups per litter. This species is targeted for human consumption and international ornamental trade purposes, and also subject to negative fishing. Similarly to other freshwater stingrays, this species is also exposed to several habitat degradation threats across its range. The fishing pressure and habitat degradation in some regions has led to some potential localised population declines, while in other areas the population is considered stable. However, due to its widespread distribution, only slight levels of overall population reduction of ~10–19% over the past three generation lengths (29 years) are suspected. Therefore, the Ocellate Freshwater Stingray is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Potamotrygon motoro presents considerable phenotypic variability within the ocellated species group. Both Potamotrygon amandae and Potamotrygon pantanensis were initially identified as P. motoro before being described (Loboda and Carvalho 2013). Recent molecular studies indicated the presence of more than one different species under the name Potamotrygon motoro (Garcia et al. 2016, Fontenelle et al. 2021) but these still remain undescribed.
